mappings.applicability_reason: This threat involves an automated webhook pipeline (Callback Receiver and Channel Poster) rather than a privileged administrative or operator interface used by human operators, so the conditions about an administrative interface with broad operator access do not hold for this scenario.

The Order Notifier pipeline processes HTTP callbacks and posts messages; there is no model or AI component receiving untrusted content, so the requirement about treating external content as untrusted model input does not bear on this threat.

No model output is published; the system forwards payment status callbacks to an operations channel without involving an AI component, so controls on validating model output before external publication are irrelevant to this threat.

The data flow involves callbacks and HTTP posting, not sending customer content to an external model provider, so the requirement about minimizing data sent to an external model does not apply to this threat.

There is no model whose output is rendered into a UI or markup; the operations channel receives textual status messages directly from the Channel Poster, so AI output encoding controls do not bear on this threat.

This threat concerns a machine-to-machine webhook endpoint and internal service, not end-user authentication delegated to an external identity provider, so the requirement about documenting delegated user authentication does not apply here.

No privileged administrative interface is involved in this threat; it concerns an unauthenticated webhook endpoint and an internal posting service, so multi-factor authentication responsibility for administrative access is out of scope.

The described threat is about incorrect or forged order-status callbacks being accepted and forwarded, not about tenant separation or cross-tenant data access, so tenant-aware authorization controls do not bear on this scenario.

While the Channel Poster calls an external channel platform API, the threat under evaluation is about the integrity of the order-status information it sends (driven by callbacks), not about the breadth of delegated privileges on that platform, so limiting integration scopes does not mitigate this threat path.

The threat involves runtime webhook handling and message posting, not how the system is built or deployed or how dependencies enter the pipeline, so controls on deployment pipeline trust and dependency management do not affect this scenario.

This threat is about integrity of order-status callbacks from an external provider and their acceptance without verification, not about confidentiality or encryption of data at rest or in transit, so the encryption requirement does not bear on this threat path.

Order Notifier is described as receiving callbacks and posting updates; the threat concerns immediate misrepresentation of order status, not retention of working copies or artifacts after processing, so data retention controls do not affect this scenario.

The threat path does not involve stored artifacts from multiple customers in shared storage; it concerns transient order-status callbacks and messages, so tenant separation for stored artifacts is not engaged here.

The scenario focuses on how callbacks are trusted and propagated in real time, not on how customer data is deleted on request from primary or derived stores, so deletion controls do not bear on this threat.

The impact described is that operations staff are misled by channel messages, not that sensitive data appears in logs or that log destinations are uncontrolled, so log-content controls do not mitigate this threat.

No privileged administrative interface or operator actions changing configuration are involved; the threat concerns automated processing of callbacks, so auditing of administrative actions is out of scope for this scenario.

The Callback Receiver is intentionally exposed on the internet as a public webhook endpoint registered with the payment provider (an external service), so the requirement that internal data stores, queues, or services not be publicly reachable does not apply to this deliberately public interface.

The described threat arises from accepting unsigned callbacks as authoritative, not from compromise or mishandling of long-lived signing keys or provider credentials held by the system, so managed secret storage for such credentials does not address this scenario.

This threat does not involve the system using tokens to access customer resources on an external platform; it concerns inbound callbacks from a payment provider, so the choice between short-lived and long-lived outbound credentials does not bear on this threat path.

While the payment provider is an external processor, the threat here is that incorrect status values in its callbacks are trusted and propagated, not how the provider retains or uses customer data, so the requirement about documenting provider retention and usage terms does not mitigate this scenario.

The threat focuses on the integrity of individual callbacks and resulting status messages, not on unbounded work or cost due to repeated triggers or retries against a metered external service, so the requirement to bound externally triggered work is not engaged here.

The system exposes the Callback Receiver as a webhook endpoint that accepts order-status events from an external payment provider and triggers further processing, and the threat describes that callbacks are trusted as authoritative; this matches the requirement’s conditions for endpoints that accept events from an external platform and perform work based on them.

This requirement addresses replay or duplicate delivery of otherwise authentic events where origin verification is in place; in this system callbacks are not authenticated at all (they are unsigned and accepted from anywhere), so the precondition about event authenticity being verified does not hold and replay-handling would not address the primary threat.

catalog_gap_candidates.concern: Order Notifier treats payment-provider callbacks as fully authoritative and forwards their order-status values directly to the operations channel without any independent validation (such as reconciling with an internal system of record or applying business sanity checks), so a compromised or buggy but correctly authenticated provider can still mislead operations with incorrect yet well-formed updates.

nearest_requirements.why_not: req-WEBHOOK-001 requires cryptographic verification that inbound events originate from the named external platform, but it does not address the case where the platform itself sends semantically incorrect or malicious status values that are still validly signed; it covers authenticity, not correctness of provider-supplied business data.

req-TPI-001 concerns what customer data is sent to an external processor and how that processor retains and uses it; it does not cover validating or cross-checking the correctness of status information the processor returns or the risk of treating such callbacks as an unquestioned source of truth.
